definition: Imperialism means a nation's policy of extending its power over other lands and peoples and running them for its own gain.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word imperialism. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know imperialism should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The atlas of 1900 wears imperialism on its face: half of Africa printed in the colors of four European capitals.
Expansionism is milder than imperialism: it names the appetite for more territory or markets, while imperialism is the full policy of ruling other lands and peoples once they are reached.
Subjugation goes further than imperialism: an imperial power may rule through governors, clients, and commerce, but subjugation crushes a people's own institutions until nothing answers back.

Colonization is one instrument of empire: the planting of settlers on foreign soil to hold and work it for the home country. Imperialism is the whole policy — conquest, colonies, debt, and gunboats all serve it, and it can run an 'independent' country without settling a single family there.

Expansionism names the appetite — the drive to enlarge a nation's territory, markets, or reach. Imperialism is the appetite grown into a system: not just wanting more, but ruling what is swallowed and running it from the center.

Imperialism means a nation's policy of extending its power over other lands and peoples and running them for its own gain.
The kingdom of Veyra never planted a single overseas colony, yet by 1890 its imperialism ran along two thousand miles of foreign coastline.

Client princes kept their thrones so long as Veyran advisers approved their budgets; Veyran mints printed the coastal states' coinage; and when one sultan objected, a gunboat anchored offshore until he stopped objecting.

Veyra shows why imperialism is the bigger word: it names the whole policy of commanding other lands and peoples for the home country's gain, whatever the instrument — conquest, colonies, debt, advisers, or a gunboat riding at anchor.
Settling foreign soil is one tool of that policy, but as Veyra proves, the policy never required it.

Imperialism is a charge as much as a description: a nation extending command over other lands and running them for its own gain.
Colonization, taught beside it in this unit, is one instrument of that policy — settlers planted to stay.
And when the dominance works by deference instead of command — no veto, no garrison, others simply follow — this unit's hegemony is the sharper word.

On paper the highland kingdom stayed independent, and its king reviewed the honor guard every spring.
In practice its copper left through a foreign company's port, its national bank answered to directors four thousand miles away, and its budget came back approved or trimmed by a distant ministry.
Not one foreign regiment was stationed there, and not one shipload of settlers ever arrived.
Historians offer the kingdom as a textbook case of imperialism, though the word never appears in its treaties.
